diagrams.name: anat-p244-primary-vs-permanent-molar
diagrams.title: Mesiodistal section: primary vs permanent mandibular first molar

cloze.text: Both the curve of Spee and the curve of Wilson are anatomic curvatures forming a line similar to an {{c1::upward smile line}}.
The {{c1::curve of Spee}} is the {{c2::anteroposterior}} curvature of the occlusal surfaces, seen from the {{c3::buccal}} aspect.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Spee → S like Side → Side view is Spee.

cloze.text: The {{c1::curve of Wilson}} is the {{c2::mesiolateral}} curve, seen from the {{c3::frontal}} view, that contacts the buccal and lingual {{c4::cusp tips}} of the arch.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: ForWard → Frontal view is Wilson.

cloze.text: The curve of Wilson forms an upward arch because the {{c1::buccal}} cusps are higher than the {{c2::lingual}} cusps on the mandibular teeth.
{{c1::Overjet}}: the maxillary teeth project over the mandibular teeth in a {{c2::horizontal}} direction.
Overjet distance is measured with the probe held {{c1::horizontally}}.
{{c1::Overbite}}: the maxillary teeth overlap the anterior mandibular teeth in a {{c2::vertical}} direction.
Overbite is measured with the probe held {{c1::vertically}}.
{{c1::Edge-to-edge}} relationship (anterior teeth): {{c2::no overjet or overbite}} — the anterior teeth meet in a straight line.
{{c1::End-to-end}} relationship (posterior teeth): no overbite — the posterior teeth are {{c2::stacked on top of one another}}.
{{c1::Open bite}}: {{c2::no vertical overlap}} of the lower incisors by the upper incisors (can also occur in posterior teeth).
Open bite is often associated with {{c1::tongue thrust}}.
{{c1::Crossbite}}: malocclusion in which a tooth (or teeth) has a more {{c2::buccal or lingual}} position than its corresponding antagonist tooth in the opposite arch.
In a (posterior) crossbite, the {{c1::maxillary}} teeth fall {{c2::inside}} the mandibular teeth on one side.
An {{c1::anterior crossbite}} shows the maxillary anterior teeth falling {{c2::behind}} the mandibular anteriors.

Angle classification is based on the relationship of the {{c1::mesiobuccal cusp}} of the permanent {{c2::maxillary first molar}} and the {{c3::buccal groove}} of the permanent {{c4::mandibular first molar}}.
Class I {{c1::neutrocclusion}}: the MB cusp of the max 1st molar fits in the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar, with {{c2::normal overbite and overjet and no rotation or crowding}}.
Class I {{c1::malocclusion}}: normal molar relationship (MB cusp of the max 1st molar fits in the buccal groove of the mand 1st molar), but {{c2::crowding, crossbite, etc.}} is present.
Angle Class {{c1::II}}: the MB cusp of the max 1st molar is {{c2::in front of (mesial to)}} the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar.
cloze.extra: Answer key: maxillary first molar is mesial to its normal position (overbite).

cloze.text: Class II, Division {{c1::I}}: upper incisors {{c2::protruded}} (out).
Class II, Division {{c1::II}}: upper incisors {{c2::retruded}} (in).
Angle Class {{c1::III}}: the MB cusp of the max 1st molar is {{c2::behind (distal to)}} the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar.
cloze.extra: Answer key: maxillary first molar is distal to its normal position (underbite/prognathism).

cloze.text: {{c1::Linguoversion}}: tooth is tipped toward the {{c2::tongue}}.
{{c1::Buccoversion}}: tooth is tipped toward the {{c2::cheek}} (term used for {{c3::posterior}} teeth).
{{c1::Labioversion}}: tooth is tipped toward the {{c2::lip}} (term used for {{c3::anterior}} teeth).
{{c1::Torsiversion}}: tooth is {{c2::rotated or twisted on its axis}}.
{{c1::Supraversion}}: tooth is {{c2::overerupted}}, extending above the occlusal plane.
{{c1::Infraversion}}: tooth is {{c2::undererupted or submerged}} below the occlusal plane.
{{c1::Transversion}} (transposition): tooth has erupted into the {{c2::wrong position}}, often swapped with another tooth.
The primary dentition has {{c1::20}} teeth: {{c2::8}} incisors, {{c3::4}} canines, and {{c4::8}} molars.
The primary dentition begins with eruption of the primary {{c1::mandibular central incisor}} at around {{c2::6–10 months}}.
The primary dentition is completed with eruption of the primary {{c1::maxillary second molar}} at {{c2::25–33 months}} (about 2–3 years old).
The primary dentition lasts from {{c1::6 months to 6 years}}, ending when the {{c2::first permanent tooth}} erupts.
Compared with permanent teeth, primary teeth are {{c1::smaller}} in size and {{c2::whiter}}.
Compared with permanent teeth, primary enamel is more {{c1::consistent}} and {{c2::thinner}}.
Compared with permanent teeth, primary crowns are {{c1::shorter}} with a more {{c2::constricted}} cervical area.
Compared with permanent teeth, primary cuspal anatomy is {{c1::smoother}}.
Primary pulp chambers are {{c1::larger}}, so there is {{c2::less}} dentin than in permanent teeth.
Compared with permanent roots, primary roots are {{c1::slimmer}} and more {{c2::divergent}}.
Primary incisors may have no {{c1::mamelons}} on the incisal edges and no {{c2::pits}} on the lingual surfaces.
cloze.extra: Book wording garbled ("The incisal edges and pits on the lingual surfaces may not have mamelons"); restated.

cloze.text: Primary teeth may have {{c1::spacing}} between them, which makes oral care easier to perform.
Mixed dentition generally lasts from {{c1::6 to 12}} years of age.
Mixed dentition begins with eruption of the {{c1::first permanent tooth}}.
Mixed dentition ends when the {{c1::last primary tooth is lost}} — usually the primary {{c2::maxillary canine}} or {{c2::second primary molar}}.
During the mixed dentition the {{c1::jaw}} undergoes fast and noticeable growth.
Because there are no premolars in the primary dentition, the primary molars are replaced by permanent {{c1::premolars}}.
If primary teeth are lost before the permanent teeth are ready to replace them, posterior teeth may {{c1::drift forward}} and occupy the space meant for permanent teeth.
The permanent dentition has {{c1::32}} teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, {{c2::8}} premolars, and {{c3::12}} molars.
The permanent dentition begins with the {{c1::shedding of the last primary tooth}}.
{{c1::Succedaneous}} teeth have primary predecessors; in the permanent dentition these are the {{c2::anterior and premolar}} teeth.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: replace "succedaneous" with "following" — a nonsuccedaneous tooth does not follow any primary tooth.

cloze.text: Succedaneous teeth erupt {{c1::lingual}} to the primary tooth, except for the permanent {{c2::maxillary incisors}}.
Permanent molars are {{c1::nonsuccedaneous}} (they do not have primary predecessors).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: a nonsuccedaneous tooth does not follow any primary tooth.

cloze.text: {{c1::Premolars}} are only present in the permanent dentition.
The permanent dentition is completed with eruption of the {{c1::third molars}} at {{c2::17 to 21}} years.
Permanent teeth are {{c1::larger}} and {{c2::yellower}} than primary teeth.
Permanent maxillary central incisor: erupts at {{c1::7–8 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::3}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary lateral incisor: erupts at {{c1::8–9 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::5}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary canine: erupts at {{c1::11–12 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::10}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary first premolar: erupts at {{c1::10–11 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::7}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary second premolar: erupts at {{c1::10–12 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::8}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary first molar: erupts at {{c1::6–7 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::1}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary second molar: erupts at {{c1::12–13 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::13}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular central incisor: erupts at {{c1::6–7 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::2}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular lateral incisor: erupts at {{c1::7–8 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::4}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular canine: erupts at {{c1::9–10 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::6}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular first premolar: erupts at {{c1::10–12 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::9}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular second premolar: erupts at {{c1::11–12 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::11}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular first molar: erupts at {{c1::6–7 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::1}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular second molar: erupts at {{c1::11–13 years}}; eruption sequence #{{c2::12}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all permanent teeth, both arches (first molars tie at #1).

cloze.text: Permanent maxillary and mandibular third molars erupt at {{c1::17–21 years}}.
Permanent maxillary eruption order: first molar → central incisor → lateral incisor → {{c1::first premolar → second premolar → canine}} → second molar → third molar.
cloze.extra: Read off the book's eruption table (sequence numbers).

cloze.text: Permanent mandibular eruption order: first molar → central incisor → lateral incisor → {{c1::canine → first premolar → second premolar}} → second molar → third molar.
cloze.extra: Read off the book's eruption table (sequence numbers).

cloze.text: Roots of the permanent teeth generally take about {{c1::2–3 years}} after eruption to complete growing — a clue for estimating a child's age on a radiograph.
cloze.extra: Did you know: e.g. permanent mandibular first molar erupted with roots about complete → 6 years + 3 years = about 9 years old.

cloze.text: In general, the {{c1::mandibular}} teeth erupt earlier than their maxillary counterparts.
Maxillary permanent canines usually erupt {{c1::after the premolars}}.
The {{c1::maxillary canine}} is the longest tooth in the dentition and requires more time to form.
Primary maxillary central incisor: erupts at {{c1::8–12 months}} (sequence #{{c2::2}}); shed at {{c3::6–7 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary maxillary lateral incisor: erupts at {{c1::9–13 months}} (sequence #{{c2::3}}); shed at {{c3::7–8 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary maxillary canine: erupts at {{c1::16–22 months}} (sequence #{{c2::7}}); shed at {{c3::10–12 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary maxillary first molar: erupts at {{c1::13–19 months}} (sequence #{{c2::5}}); shed at {{c3::9–11 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary maxillary second molar: erupts at {{c1::25–33 months}} (sequence #{{c2::10}}); shed at {{c3::10–12 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary mandibular central incisor: erupts at {{c1::6–10 months}} (sequence #{{c2::1}}); shed at {{c3::6–7 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary mandibular lateral incisor: erupts at {{c1::10–16 months}} (sequence #{{c2::4}}); shed at {{c3::7–8 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary mandibular canine: erupts at {{c1::17–23 months}} (sequence #{{c2::8}}); shed at {{c3::9–12 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary mandibular first molar: erupts at {{c1::14–18 months}} (sequence #{{c2::6}}); shed at {{c3::9–11 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary mandibular second molar: erupts at {{c1::23–31 months}} (sequence #{{c2::9}}); shed at {{c3::10–12 years}}.
cloze.extra: Sequence = order of eruption among all primary teeth, both arches.

cloze.text: Primary eruption order by tooth type: central incisor → lateral incisor → {{c1::first molar}} → {{c2::canine}} → second molar.
cloze.extra: From the book's primary-dentition sketch (numbered 1–5).

cloze.text: {{c1::Endogenous}} stain occurs during tooth development.
{{c1::Exogenous}} stain occurs after tooth eruption.
{{c1::Intrinsic}} stain is located within the tooth; it {{c2::cannot}} be removed by scaling and/or polishing but may be reduced by {{c3::whitening}}.
{{c1::Extrinsic}} stain is located on the surface of the tooth and {{c2::can}} be removed by scaling and/or polishing.
Over time, extrinsic stain can become {{c1::intrinsic}}.
{{c1::Fluorosis}} is caused by excessive {{c2::fluoride}} consumption.
Fluorosis can appear as {{c1::white/brown spots, milky opalescence, pitting, and mottling}}.
{{c1::Tetracycline}} stain is caused by ingestion of the antibiotic by the {{c2::pregnant or lactating mother}}.
cloze.extra: Also occurs when the child takes it while teeth are forming (generally under age 8).

cloze.text: Tetracycline-stained teeth can be {{c1::yellow/brown}} and {{c2::fluoresce}} under {{c3::ultraviolet}} light (fluorescence ceases with age).
{{c1::Minocycline}} (a tetracycline derivative) can create a {{c2::bluish-gray}} stain.
{{c1::Pulp necrosis}} creates {{c2::dark}} teeth.
{{c1::Pulpitis}} creates {{c2::pink}} discoloration, caused by inflammation and internal bleeding in the pulp chamber.
Other endogenous intrinsic stains include {{c1::amelogenesis imperfecta}}, {{c2::dentinogenesis imperfecta}}, and {{c3::enamel hypoplasia}}.
{{c1::Amalgam}} staining: {{c2::silver}} from the restoration leaches into the tooth structure and causes {{c3::gray to black}} staining.
Caries discolor the tooth surface; {{c1::arrested}} caries can present as {{c2::black}} stain that cannot be removed.
{{c1::Endodontic therapy}} can also lead to intrinsic staining of the tooth.
{{c1::Yellow}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::heavy dental biofilm buildup}}.
{{c1::Green}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::poor oral hygiene}} or {{c3::Nasmyth's membrane}}.
{{c1::Nasmyth's membrane}} is thin tissue on newly erupted teeth, which will brush off.
{{c1::Black line}} stain is caused by {{c2::iron compounds}} embedded in dental biofilm and is found in {{c3::clean}} mouths.
{{c1::Brown to black}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::tobacco}} use (smoking or chewing).
{{c1::Orange}} extrinsic stain is associated with {{c2::chromogenic bacteria}}.
{{c1::Tan to dark brown}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::food}} such as red wine, tea, or coffee.
{{c1::Yellow, brown, or gray}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::chlorhexidine}}.
{{c1::Gray-green}} extrinsic stain is caused by {{c2::marijuana}}.
The Universal system uses numbers {{c1::1 to 32}} for the permanent dentition and letters {{c2::A to T}} for the primary dentition.
Universal numbering starts at the {{c1::maxillary right third molar}}, moves {{c2::clockwise}}, and ends with the {{c3::mandibular right third molar}}.
In the Universal system, the mandibular right central incisor is #{{c1::25}}.
The Universal system is used primarily in the {{c1::United States}}.
The {{c1::ISO (FDI)}} designation system is used in Canada, Europe, etc., and is accepted by the {{c2::WHO}}.
The ISO/FDI system uses a {{c1::two-digit}} number for each tooth.
In ISO/FDI, the first digit indicates the {{c1::quadrant}} — {{c2::1–4}} for permanent and {{c3::5–8}} for primary teeth — numbered in a clockwise direction.
In ISO/FDI, the second digit indicates the tooth in the quadrant (1–{{c1::8}} for permanent, 1–{{c2::5}} for primary); number 1 is closest to the {{c3::midline}}.
ISO #17 (1.7) = Universal #{{c1::2}}; ISO #61 (6.1) = Universal #{{c2::F}}.
The {{c1::Palmer}} system designates teeth with a {{c2::right-angle symbol}} indicating the quadrant, with the tooth number inside.
In the Palmer system, permanent teeth are numbered {{c1::1–8}} and primary teeth lettered {{c2::A–E}}, counting from the midline in each quadrant.
cloze.extra: Read off the book's charts.

cloze.text: The Palmer system is used especially in {{c1::orthodontics}}.
The Palmer system can produce an immediate {{c1::graphical map}} of the dentition.

mcq.question: Which tooth typically has the prominent cusp of Carabelli?
mcq.explanation: The cusp of Carabelli is a fifth supplemental cusp found on the mesiolingual cusp of the maxillary first molar, most commonly on the permanent first molar. It is not typically found on incisors, premolars, or mandibular molars.

mcq.question: Which permanent tooth is likely to be congenitally missing?
mcq.explanation: The most commonly missing permanent teeth are the third molars, followed by the maxillary lateral incisors, then the mandibular second premolars.

mcq.question: Which root of a maxillary first molar is the longest?
options: D. All are equal in length
mcq.explanation: The palatal root of the maxillary first molar is typically the longest and largest, providing significant anchorage. The mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots are shorter and located on the buccal side.

mcq.question: What is the smallest permanent tooth in the mouth?
mcq.explanation: The mandibular central incisor is the smallest permanent tooth, both in crown width and root size.

mcq.question: A patient presents with a large maxillary incisor that appears to have a notch on the incisal edge and an unusually wide crown. A radiograph reveals a single root canal. Which best describes this condition?
options: A. Fusion, with a normal tooth count
B. Fusion, with one tooth missing in the arch
C. Gemination, with a normal tooth count
D. Gemination, with one tooth missing in the arch
mcq.answer: C. Gemination, with a normal tooth count
mcq.explanation:
Gemination occurs when a single tooth bud attempts to divide, resulting in a large tooth with a bifid crown (notched or partially separated) but typically only one root and one pulp canal; the total tooth count is normal when the anomalous tooth is counted as one.
Fusion, by contrast, is the union of two separate tooth buds, usually resulting in a large tooth with two pulp canals and a reduced tooth count (when the fused teeth are counted as one).

mcq.question: Which best describes a clinical and radiographic feature of internal resorption?
options: A. Pink discoloration of the crown and a round, symmetrical radiolucency in the pulp chamber
B. Pink discoloration of the crown and an asymmetrical radiolucency on the root surface
C. Normal tooth color and a radiolucency that shifts position on angled radiographs
D. Gray discoloration of the crown and widened periodontal ligament space
mcq.answer: A. Pink discoloration of the crown and a round, symmetrical radiolucency in the pulp chamber
mcq.explanation: Internal resorption often causes a "pink tooth of Mummery" — a pink hue visible through the enamel due to vascular granulation tissue in the pulp chamber. Radiographically it appears as a well-defined, symmetrical radiolucency centered in the pulp space.

mcq.question: According to Angle's classification of occlusion, which describes a Class II molar relationship?
options: A. The mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar occludes with the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar
B. The mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar is positioned mesial to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar
C. The mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar is positioned distal to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar
D. The mesiobuccal cusp of the mandibular first molar occludes with the central fossa of the maxillary first molar
mcq.answer: B. The mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar is positioned mesial to the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar
mcq.explanation:
Angle's Class I: normal — MB cusp of the maxillary first molar aligns with the buccal groove of the mandibular first molar.
Class II: maxillary first molar is mesial to its normal position (overbite).
Class III: maxillary first molar is distal to its normal position (underbite/prognathism).

mcq.question: A child presents with all four maxillary and mandibular permanent incisors erupted, but no permanent canines or premolars. Based on typical eruption patterns, what is the most likely age range of this patient?
mcq.explanation: Permanent central incisors usually erupt around 6–8 years, and lateral incisors around 7–9 years. Permanent canines and premolars typically erupt after age 9, around 10–12 years. So a child with the 4 permanent incisors erupted is most likely 8–9 years old.
